title: IPv6
summary: IPv4 ran out of addresses. IPv6 fixes that with a 128-bit space, a cleaner header, and built-in features that IPv4 had to bolt on later.

blocks.markdown:
**IPv6** is the successor to [ipv4-addressing](ipv4-addressing), built to fix one core problem: the internet ran out of IPv4 addresses.

- Uses **128-bit** addresses instead of 32-bit — far more space.
- Written in **hexadecimal**, grouped in eight 16-bit blocks.
- Simpler header, no broadcast, built-in features like NDP.
- Deployed alongside IPv4 today via dual-stack and tunneling.

blocks.subTitle: IPv4 vs IPv6 at a glance
blocks.markdown:
Key differences side by side.

| Feature | IPv4 | IPv6 |
|---|---|---|
| Address size | 32-bit | 128-bit |
| Notation | Decimal dotted | Hex colon-separated |
| Broadcast | Yes | No |
| Header size | 20–60 bytes | Fixed 40 bytes |

**IPv4 exhaustion** drove the need for IPv6.

- IPv4 has 2³² ≈ 4.3 billion addresses. By the 2010s, the global pool was gone.
- Workarounds like **NAT** (Network Address Translation) let many devices share one IP, but they break end-to-end connectivity and add complexity.
- IPv6 has 2¹²⁸ ≈ 340 undecillion addresses — enough to give every atom on Earth an address many times over.

An IPv6 address is **128 bits** written as eight groups of four hex digits, separated by colons.

```
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
```

- Each group is **16 bits** (four hex digits, 0–9 and a–f).
- Hex is used because writing 128 bits in decimal would be unwieldy.
- Compare: IPv4 is four decimal octets like `192.168.1.1`.

blocks.subTitle: Shortening rules
blocks.markdown:
Two rules make IPv6 addresses shorter to write.

**Rule 1 — Drop leading zeros** in each group: `0db8` → `db8`, `0000` → `0`.

**Rule 2 — `::` replaces one consecutive run of all-zero groups** (used once per address).

```
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
→  2001:db8::1
```

blocks.subTitle: Unicast, multicast, anycast
blocks.markdown:
IPv6 has three address types — broadcast is gone.

- **Unicast** — one sender to one receiver. Same as a normal IPv4 address.
- **Multicast** — one sender to a **group** of subscribed receivers. Replaces broadcast.
- **Anycast** — one address assigned to multiple devices; packets go to the **nearest** one. Used for load balancing and DNS.

blocks.subTitle: Link-local addresses
blocks.markdown:
A **link-local** address is a unicast address that is only valid on a single network segment — packets with this address are never routed.

- Always starts with `fe80::/10`.
- Every IPv6 interface generates one automatically from its MAC address.
- Used for neighbor discovery and router communication before a global address is assigned.

IPv6 eliminates **broadcast** — the old IPv4 mechanism where one packet floods every device on a subnet.

- Broadcast wastes bandwidth: every host must process the packet, even if it has nothing to do with it.
- IPv6 replaces it with **multicast**: only subscribed hosts receive the packet.
- This reduces unnecessary interruptions and makes large networks more efficient.

IPv6 improved the protocol in several areas beyond just address size.

| Area | IPv4 | IPv6 |
|---|---|---|
| Security | Optional (IPsec add-on) | IPsec built-in |
| Header | Variable, complex | Fixed 40-byte, simpler |
| Config | DHCP needed | Stateless auto-config (SLAAC) |

blocks.subTitle: Simpler header
blocks.markdown:
The IPv6 header is **fixed at 40 bytes** and has fewer fields than IPv4's variable-length header.

- IPv4 has a checksum field recalculated at every router hop — slow.
- IPv6 **drops the checksum** (transport layers like TCP/UDP already have checksums).
- Fragmentation is handled by the **sender**, not routers, making forwarding faster.
- Optional extension headers chain after the fixed header as needed.

The internet can't switch to IPv6 overnight — both protocols run in parallel via transition mechanisms.

- **Dual stack** — a device runs both IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time. It speaks whichever version the destination supports. Most modern OS and routers are dual-stack today.
- **Tunneling** — wraps IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets to cross IPv4-only networks. The IPv6 packet is the payload; the outer header is IPv4.

**NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol)** replaces ARP and adds more functions.

- **ARP** (IPv4) broadcasts a request to find the MAC address for an IP. IPv6 has no broadcast, so NDP uses **multicast** instead.
- NDP handles: MAC discovery, router discovery, stateless address auto-configuration (**SLAAC**), and duplicate address detection (**DAD**).
- Runs on top of ICMPv6. See [network-fundamentals](network-fundamentals) for how ARP worked.

Common misconceptions:

- **":: can appear twice."** No — `::` can only be used once per address; otherwise you can't tell how many zeros each `::` expands to.
- **"IPv6 eliminated NAT entirely."** Not yet — NAT is discouraged but still used for security reasons.
- **"IPv4 is being turned off."** No — dual-stack keeps both alive; IPv4 isn't going away soon.

blocks.subTitle: Why IPv6
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why was IPv6 created?**

IPv4's 32-bit space (~4.3 billion addresses) was exhausted. NAT extended its life but broke end-to-end connectivity. IPv6's 128-bit space is effectively unlimited and also brings a cleaner header, built-in IPsec, and multicast replacing broadcast.

blocks.subTitle: Shortening an address
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you shorten an IPv6 address?**

Two steps: (1) drop leading zeros in each group — `0db8` → `db8`. (2) replace the longest consecutive run of all-zero groups with `::` — but only once. `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001` → `2001:db8::1`.

blocks.subTitle: What replaced ARP and broadcast
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What replaced ARP and broadcast in IPv6?**

**NDP** (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) replaced ARP. It uses ICMPv6 multicast instead of broadcast to find MAC addresses, discover routers, and auto-configure addresses (SLAAC). Broadcast itself is replaced entirely by multicast.

blocks.subTitle: Dual stack vs tunneling
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is dual stack, and how does tunneling differ?**

**Dual stack**: a device runs IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously and uses whichever the destination supports — no translation needed. **Tunneling**: wraps IPv6 packets inside IPv4 for legs of the path that only speak IPv4. Dual stack is preferred; tunneling is a fallback.

blocks.subTitle: IPv4 vs IPv6 header
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does the IPv6 header improve on IPv4?**

IPv6's header is **fixed at 40 bytes** with no checksum (removing per-hop recalculation) and no fragmentation fields (moved to extension headers, handled by senders). Fewer fields mean routers forward packets faster.
